content: Urinary incontinence is a prevalent and distressing condition that significantly impacts quality of life. Bladder training is a behavioral intervention designed to increase the time interval between voiding episodes and is commonly employed as a treatment for urinary incontinence. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of bladder training in managing urinary incontinence. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register as of March 15, 2006. Additional sources included reference lists of relevant articles and direct communication with trial investigators to identify other potential studies. The review focused on randomized or quasi-randomized trials that assessed bladder training for any type of urinary incontinence. Two independent reviewers evaluated the quality of the trials and extracted data. Five primary outcomes were predefined: participants' perception of cure, participants' perception of improvement, the number of incontinent episodes, the number of micturitions, and quality of life. Adverse events were also recorded. The review compared three scenarios: bladder training versus no bladder training, bladder training versus other treatments, and bladder training combined with another treatment versus that other treatment alone. A total of 109 reports from 60 potentially relevant trials were identified, of which 31 reports from 12 trials met the inclusion criteria. These trials involved 1,473 participants, predominantly women. Eight trials, including 858 participants with urinary incontinence at baseline, were included in the analysis. The quality of the trials varied, and there was limited data on long-term follow-up. Bladder training versus no bladder training: Three trials involving 172 women compared bladder training with no bladder training. These trials reported a limited number of predefined outcomes, which varied across studies. While the point estimates of effect generally favored bladder training, the confidence intervals were wide, and no statistically significant differences were observed for the primary outcomes. Bladder training versus other treatments: Three trials involving 159 women compared bladder training with pharmacological treatments. Two trials evaluated bladder training against oxybutynin, and one trial compared it with a combination of imipramine and flavoxate. In the trials with oxybutynin, bladder training showed statistically significant benefits in participants' perception of cure at six months (relative risk [RR] 1.69; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.21 to 2.34) and quality of life (weighted mean difference [WMD] 9.00; 95% CI 1.64 to 16.36). However, drug treatment was favored for reducing the number of daytime micturitions per week (WMD 2.80; 95% CI 0.91 to 4.69). Adverse events were more common with drug treatment. In the trial comparing bladder training with imipramine plus flavoxate, participants' perception of cure immediately after treatment was statistically significant in favor of bladder training (RR 1.50; 95% CI 1.02 to 2.21), and this benefit persisted at approximately two months post-treatment. Two additional trials compared bladder training with pelvic floor muscle training combined with biofeedback in 164 women, but no statistically significant differences were found in the primary outcomes. Bladder training combined with another treatment versus that treatment alone: Two trials involving 331 participants compared the combination of bladder training and an anticholinergic drug with the drug alone. In the largest trial, data were available for only one predefined outcome: the median number of incontinent episodes, which was the same in both groups. Another trial compared pelvic floor muscle training plus biofeedback supplemented with bladder training versus pelvic floor muscle training plus biofeedback alone in 125 women. In this trial, participants' perception of improvement and quality of life immediately after treatment showed statistically significant benefits for the group receiving the combined intervention (perception of improvement: RR 1.18; 95% CI 1.01 to 1.39; quality of life: mean difference [MD] -47.20; 95% CI -87.03 to -7.37). However, these benefits were not sustained at three months. Conclusions: The available evidence suggests that bladder training may be beneficial for the treatment of urinary incontinence. However, this conclusion is tentative due to the variable quality of the trials, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals around the effect estimates. Additionally, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether bladder training is effective as an adjunct to other therapies. Further high-quality research is needed to establish definitive conclusions.
